Article Title: Leavitt to leave White House podium to become MAGA warrior mom
Article Text:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt

The TOI correspondent from Washington:

For a White House that has never been shy about deploying its best-looking and sharpest tongue, Karoline Leavitt was something of a two-for-one political bargain: the photogenic face of the Trump White House, vaporising critical reporters with verbal volleys before they finished the question. Now the show is over -- at least from the WH podium.The 28-year-old press secretary announced Wednesday that she will depart her job at the end of August, saying motherhood had finally trumped mouthing for the Trump White House. “Being a mother and welcoming a new baby while working in one of the most demanding jobs in the world has been the most rewarding yet challenging season of my life,” she wrote on X. After returning from maternity leave only on July 16, she said she had concluded she could not be “the best mom my two young children deserve” while giving the press secretary’s job the “constant time, energy, and attention” it demands.That is the official explanation; Washington, never short of scuttlebutt and speculation, produced several unofficial ones. The most colorful theory: Leavitt's maternal epiphany was not the only thing that happened to her in Turkey. Apparently, during Trump's recent departure from Ankara when he was shipped out in a catering container, Leavitt was left behind on the decoy plane while Natalie Harp, a Trump whisperer who is said to manage some of his social media posting, got to ride with the President.Add the fact that Leavitt's resignation came almost immediately after the bizarre flight became public, and social media did what it does best: connected two dots and declared it a constellation.There is, however, no credible evidence that the airplane episode caused Leavitt's resignation, nor evidence of the alleged argument with Trump or Harp. The timing has fueled speculation, but timing is not proof. On her part, Leavitt expressed gratitude to Trump for the "honor and adventure of a lifetime, revealing that he has "asked me to continue serving as a top advisor to him on the outside, and I will always remain a vocal advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party. "Trump's own explanation contains a delicious little Washington contradiction. He said Leavitt was leaving so she could spend more time with her “beautiful young children and family” – a decision he “totally understands and respects.” Yet, in the same breath, he declared she would become one of his “top outside advisors” and “an influential voice” in the GOP as Republicans seek to win the November midterms.In other words: Congratulations, Karoline, you're free from the White House — effective immediately, please report to the Republican campaign war room.Leavitt's political resume hardly suggests retirement. She entered Trump's orbit in 2018, worked in his first White House communications operation, later headed comms for Congresswoman Elise Stefanik, and ran unsuccessfully for Congress in New Hampshire in 2022. She became Trump's national press secretary during the 2024 campaign and, at 27, became the youngest person ever to hold the White House press secretary's job.At the podium, she quickly established her trademark style: combative, confident and unmistakably Trumpian. She attacked what she called “fake news,” challenged reporters aggressively and became an energetic advocate for the administration. She also helped usher podcasts, influencers and other “new media” outlets into a briefing room long dominated by the legacy media.Indeed, her influence extended well beyond the lectern. She participated in high-level meetings and briefings and became one of Trump's most trusted public defenders. Her own legacy, therefore, may be less about the number of briefings she conducted than about the changing job she embodied: press secretary as partisan warrior, rapid-response operative and political influencer, rather than merely the White House's human answering machine.And her future? Trump has already supplied the answer. Leavitt says her “fight is entering a new phase, but it is far from over.” So motherhood may be taking her out of the West Wing, but if Trump gets his way, it certainly isn't taking her out of the fight. So long, Press Secretary. Hello, MAGA mouthpiece.
Article Summary: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt announced Wednesday that she will depart her job at the end of August. She said she had concluded she could not be “the best mom my two young children deserve” while giving the press secretary’s job the “constant time, energy, and attention”

Article Title: Potatoes 'boiling' in ground, livestock dead: Record heat ruins harvest in South Korea, Japan, Hong Kong
Article Text:
Record heat hits farms as Asia endures extreme summer (Representative image)

South Korea recorded its hottest summer on record this year, with the southeastern city of Yangsan reaching 42.5°C on August 2, the highest temperature recorded in the country since modern weather observations began in 1904.A South Korean potato farmer in Gangwon province has seen his crop destroyed by extreme heat, with potatoes harvested in Yanggu county turning soft and collapsing within a week after initially appearing healthy.Farmer Lee Sang-hyuk said the tubers had become “like boiled potatoes” as intense heat affected the soil.“It’s not just one or two fields like this. How can I even put it into words? It’s so upsetting,” Sang-hyuk told local broadcaster SBS.The extreme heat has been blamed for at least 31 deaths nationwide, according to South Korea’s disease control agency, while more than 900,000 livestock and 1.4 million farmed fish have also died.Authorities issued a heat warning, urging people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung told his cabinet that the extreme weather was “unlike anything we have experienced before”.“We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system,” he said, “since this extreme weather is becoming the new normal.”In neighbouring Japan, temperatures reached 40°C or higher in several locations, while the country recorded its first “kokushobi”, or “cruelly hot day”, a new category introduced this year by the weather agency for temperatures above 40°C. In Tokyo, three lions at a city zoo died of suspected heatstroke, as cited by The Guardian.Scientists say the extreme temperatures are part of a wider pattern. Researchers at Japan’s Weather Attribution Centre found that the country’s intense July heat would have been “virtually impossible” without global warming.They estimated that, without human-caused warming, a heatwave of this scale would occur on average once every 10,000 years.In Hong Kong, the observatory recorded 36.9°C, the highest temperature there since records began in 1884, as the outer bands of Typhoon Dolphin swept hot air across the city.The record heat also highlighted shortcomings in the city’s heat-stress warning system for outdoor workers, which remained at its lowest level despite the record temperatures.In China’s western Xinjiang region, a weather station recorded 50°C in July, while heatwaves affected the country’s north-east. North Korea also reported a run of tropical nights in Pyongyang, with temperatures remaining above 25°C.The extreme heat came even as an El Niño event was under way, a natural climate pattern that has previously been linked to a lower likelihood of extreme summer heat in Japan.El Niño occurs naturally in the Pacific and, when combined with human-driven global warming, can contribute to temperature spikes and more extreme weather.
Article Summary: Temperatures in South Korea hit 42.5°C, the highest since records began in 1904. At least 31 people have died in the country due to the extreme heat. More than 900,000 livestock and 1.4 million farmed fish have also died.

Article Title: Photos: Total solar eclipse returns to Spain after more than a century, darkens skies across Europe
Article Text:
the moon covered the sun over Spain, and a total solar eclipse returned to the mainland. (Photo: PTI)

A total solar eclipse is seen from Berlanga de Duero, central Spain, Wednesday. (Photo: AP)

Sequence of the moon covering the sun in a total solar eclipse seen from Berlanga de Duero, central Spain, Wednesday, (Photo: AP)

Europe watches daylight fade

A couple talk during a solar eclipse on the shore of the Gulf of Finland in St. Petersburg, Russia, Wednesday. (Photo: AP)

A partial solar eclipse is seen above the Houses of Parliament in London, Wednesday. (Photo: AP)

Iceland becomes Europe’s first major stage for totality

Stages of a solar eclipse before, during and after totality, as seen from Arija. (Photo: Reuters)

Shadow reaches Spain as the sun begins to set

The moon moves out of the sun during a total solar eclipse is seen from Berlanga de Duero, central Spain, Wednesday. (Photo: AP)

The moon partially covers the sun during a solar eclipse over mountains near the northern Spanish town of Reinosa, Wednesday. (Reuters)

After a century-long gap, Spain waits only a year

People observe a partial solar eclipse with special protective glasses in Berlin, Germany, Wednesday. (Photo: AP)

A wait for more than a century came down to barely a minute: the moon covered the sun over Spain, and a total solar eclipse returned to the mainland. Near sunset on Wednesday, crowds watched the sky darken almost to night before sunlight briefly returned, leaving one of Europe’s rarest celestial events over almost as soon as it had begun.The rarity went deeper than Wednesday’s spectacle. Western Europe had not witnessed a total solar eclipse since 1999, while Spain’s own history carries an unusual qualification. News agency Associated Press reported that a hybrid eclipse produced only a few seconds of totality in 1912, leading some astronomers to regard 1905 as Spain’s previous full-scale total solar eclipse.From St Petersburg to Berlin, millions outside the narrow path of totality experienced a different version of the eclipse. People gathered along the Gulf of Finland in St Petersburg, while Berliners watched through protective glasses at Tempelhof and near the Molecule Man sculpture as the moon steadily covered more of the solar disc without completely blocking the sun.The effect grew stronger farther west. In Britain, more than 90% of the sun was obscured, leaving only a narrow strip of light visible at the eclipse’s peak. At Greenwich Park in London, spectators watched the sky turn grey as hilltops, parks and other open viewpoints filled with people following the changing light towards evening.Cloud covered much of the sky over central Reykjavik, but it could not disguise what was happening below. Around Hallgrímskirkja, hundreds who had gathered despite the rain saw daylight fall sharply as totality arrived; many had only a limited view of the sun itself, yet the sudden darkness and the return of light drew cheers from the crowd.Conditions farther west gave a clearer measure of the eclipse. News agency Reuters reported that totality reached Iceland’s westernmost coast at about 5.44pm local time and lasted up to 2 minutes 13 seconds. Its maximum duration, about 2 minutes 18 seconds, occurred offshore west of Iceland before the moon’s shadow continued across the North Atlantic towards Spain.After crossing the North Atlantic, the moon’s shadow reached northwestern Spain at around 8.28pm local time, bringing places including A Coruña and Bilbao into totality shortly before sunset. The timing created an extraordinary natural sequence: the sun disappeared completely, returned briefly as the moon moved on and then sank towards the horizon as evening took over.Farther inland, totality lasted barely a minute in Buitrago de Lozoya, north of Madrid. Around 8.30pm, spectators saw Baily’s beads — separate points of sunlight appearing along the moon’s edge — form close to the horizon. Cheers followed as darkness lifted and sunlight returned, only for the approaching sunset to begin dimming the sky again.In Medinaceli, spectators gathered across a Roman-era hilltop town well before the eclipse, while elsewhere in Spain people carried chairs and umbrellas into open viewing areas. The light weakened gradually before dropping rapidly as totality arrived, prompting applause and cheers from crowds watching across northern and central parts of the country.The shadow briefly clipped northeastern Portugal before reaching Spain’s Mediterranean coast and the Balearic Islands at sunset. Yet Wednesday’s eclipse begins rather than ends an unusual run for the country: another total solar eclipse will cross Spain on August 2, 2027, followed by an annular, or “ring of fire”, eclipse on January 26, 2028. After waiting more than a century, Spain now has less than 12 months to wait for totality again.
Article Summary: The moon covered the sun over Spain, and a total solar eclipse returned to the mainland. Western Europe had not witnessed atotal solar eclipse since 1999. The moon’s shadow reached northwestern Spain at around 8.28pm local time, bringing places including A Coruña and Bilbao into totality.

Article Title: ICE agents to get electric shock gloves worth $20 million to remove 'illegal aliens' from US; sparks outrage
Article Text:
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) notice was published Monday

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to spend up to $20 million on electric shock gloves for officers and agents, prompting criticism from Democratic lawmakers and civil rights advocates who warn the devices could be misused during immigration enforcement.A US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) notice published Monday said ICE plans to buy the Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, or GLOVE, for Homeland Security Investigations and Enforcement Removal Operations officers and agents. The proposed spending is between $10 million and $20 million.The gloves can deliver up to 380 volts and are designed to disrupt an individual's ability to respond, news outlet BBC reported. DHS describes them as “a Conductive Distraction and De-escalation Device”. The gloves look like ordinary patrol gloves until an officer presses a button to activate the electrical mode. News agency AP explained that they must be applied directly to a person's skin and are intended to cause pain and gain compliance from someone resisting. Unlike Tasers, they do not leave burn or contact marks.The plan quickly drew criticism from rights groups. The American Civil Liberties Union said giving immigration agents “a concealed means of delivering terrible pain is a recipe for more harm to the public and less accountability.”New York attorney general Letitia James told AP on Wednesday, “We are outraged,” warning that ICE officers who misuse the gloves in her state could face criminal and civil consequences.DHS did not specifically explain why ICE had selected the gloves but defended its broader equipment policy.“ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country,” the department said.“Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards.”Concerns have also focused on previous allegations involving the devices. A pending lawsuit alleges that a 43-year-old man died at a jail in Richmond, Kentucky, in 2024 after being shocked 27 times with the gloves and 13 more times with a Taser.An internal investigation found two glove shocks lasted 45 and 99 seconds, exceeding the manufacturer's recommended 15-second limit.“These actions not only inflicted unnecessary pain but also heightened the risk of serious health complications,” the investigation said, according to court documents.Former ICE acting director John Sandweg warned about potential misuse. “It's too easy for this to get misused, against a population that doesn't pose a threat,” he told MS NOW.The manufacturer warns against using the devices on elderly people, small children, pregnant women and severely handicapped people. Its manual also prohibits their use for verbal defiance, punishment, torture or horseplay.ICE says its officers receive de-escalation and ongoing use-of-force training. The proposed no-bid contract could be released as early as Friday and run through March 31, 2027, according to the DHS notice.
Article Summary: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to spend up to $20 million on electric shock gloves for officers and agents. The gloves can deliver up to 380 volts and are designed to disrupt an individual's ability to respond. The plan quickly drew criticism from rights groups who warn the devices could be misused during immigration enforcement.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Bubba Smith: "Well, I'm not a violent person. You have to back off. People sometimes will…" - a lesson in restraint, self-control and knowing when to step back
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Bubba Smith (Image: Wikipedia)

Quote of the day by Bubba Smith

"Well, I'm not a violent person. You have to back off. People sometimes will try you and try you until you try not to, but you have to react. Normally, I just walk away"

What this quote actually reveals about him

What the quote actually means

Why walking away can be the harder choice

Why size and strength come with real responsibility

From football to Hollywood

Why kindness and physical strength are not opposites

How to apply this lesson in daily life

Why this still resonates today

Some people assume that physical size or obvious strength naturally comes with a short temper. Bubba Smith , the former NFL defensive lineman turned actor, suggested something closer to the opposite. "Well, I'm not a violent person," he said. "You have to back off. People sometimes will try you and try you until you try not to, but you have to react. Normally, I just walk away." At six feet seven inches tall, Smith understood better than most exactly how much weight his own actions could carry, and he chose restraint as his default, a choice that says considerably more about real strength than his imposing size ever did on its own.Smith made a related point elsewhere, explaining precisely why he avoided certain situations altogether. "I don't go to clubs and stuff like that, so I don't have to put up with it in there," he said. "And normally, because obviously I could hurt somebody, and if I look at it that way, I have to back off." Read together, the two quotes paint a consistent picture, someone who was deeply aware of his own physical power and who treated that awareness as a genuine responsibility rather than something to lean on.Smith is drawing a clear line between being provoked and choosing to escalate. He is not claiming he never gets tested. He openly admits that people sometimes "try you and try you," pushing at someone repeatedly to see how far they can go. His response to that pressure was not aggression. It was walking away, treating that as the stronger, more controlled option rather than a weaker one. The quote suggests that real strength often looks like restraint rather than retaliation, particularly for someone whose size meant that any physical reaction could genuinely hurt another person.Walking away from a confrontation is often assumed to be the easy option, when in practice it can require considerably more self-control than reacting does. Someone who is repeatedly provoked has to actively choose not to respond in kind, again and again, even while their patience is being tested. For someone as physically imposing as Smith, that choice carried extra weight, since any reaction from him would have looked, and likely been, far more serious than the same reaction from someone else.Smith's comments reveal a genuine awareness that not everyone faces the same consequences for the same reaction. A smaller disagreement between two ordinary people rarely escalates into anything serious. For someone Smith's size, the stakes were different, and he seemed to recognise that directly, deliberately avoiding situations where his own presence alone might turn a minor disagreement into something far worse. That kind of self-awareness is its own form of maturity.Who was Bubba SmithBubba Smith was an American professional football player and actor, born Charles Aaron Smith on 28 February 1945. He became an outstanding defensive lineman at Michigan State University, twice earning All-American honours and playing a central role in the famous 1966 "Game of the Century," a 10-10 tie against Notre Dame. He was one of only three Michigan State players to have his jersey number retired, and he was later inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 1988. Smith was selected first overall by the Baltimore Colts in the 1967 NFL Draft, going on to a ten-year professional career that included two Super Bowl appearances and two Pro Bowl selections.Smith's career did not end when he left professional football. He became widely known in the 1970s for a series of Miller Lite beer commercials, before actually quitting the campaign himself, later explaining he felt uncomfortable being associated with encouraging alcohol use, particularly among younger viewers. He went on to build a genuinely successful acting career, best known for playing the gentle, soft-spoken Moses Hightower in the Police Academy film series, a role that used his enormous physical size for comic and warm effect rather than menace, a contrast that suited his real personality closely. He continued acting in film and television until his death in 2011.Smith's public image combined obvious physical power with a genuinely gentle screen persona, and his own words suggest that contrast was not really an act. Being capable of real force and choosing not to use it carelessly are two separate things, and his comments about walking away show someone who understood that difference clearly. Problems tend to arise only when people assume the two are the same, that someone strong must therefore be short-tempered, or that someone gentle must therefore be pushed around freely. Smith's own account suggests neither assumption held true for him.Recognise your own influence honestly, since the same reaction can land very differently depending on who delivers it. Choose restraint deliberately rather than assuming it is the passive option, since walking away often requires more discipline than reacting does. Notice when you are being tested repeatedly, and decide consciously how to respond rather than reacting purely on instinct. Avoid situations likely to escalate unnecessarily, the way Smith avoided certain places specifically because of what his own presence might provoke. And remember that genuine strength is measured as much by what someone chooses not to do as by what they are actually capable of.Smith's own words offer something more useful than a simple tough-guy line ever could, an honest account of someone large and physically powerful choosing patience as his default response, and being deliberate about the moments when he allowed himself to react at all. That restraint, chosen repeatedly rather than accidental, is really the more interesting story behind a man best remembered publicly for towering size and a gentle, likeable screen presence.
Article Summary: Bubba Smith was an American professional football player and actor. He became widely known in the 1970s for a series of Miller Lite beer commercials. He went on to build a successful acting career, best known for the gentle Hightower in the Police Academy film.

Article Title: US attack on Yemen killed 153 civilians in April 2025: Pentagon review
Article Text: A Pentagon review says US airstrikes targeting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen killed 153 civilians and injured 243 others across three attacks in April 2025. The assessment, submitted to Congress as part of the Pentagon’s annual civilian casualty report, found that the strikes “more likely than not” resulted in civilian harm.The unclassified assessment, obtained by news agency AP and reported by NBC News, examined three strikes conducted during the US military campaign against the Houthis. A Pentagon official, who was not authorised to discuss the matter publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said the department would submit the report in the coming months but had no further announcement.The findings come amid growing scrutiny of civilian casualties from US military operations under the Trump administration, including concerns raised by lawmakers in Congress.The Pentagon review focused on strikes against Houthi-controlled positions in and around Sanaa, Yemen’s rebel-held capital, and at the Ras Isa port. The assessment found that the three operations “more likely than not” resulted in civilian harm.The review said its conclusions were based on US intelligence, imagery and open-source reporting.The Ras Isa strike was the deadliest, killing 80 people and injuring 171 others.The attack triggered large fires and explosions at the port, with tanker trucks left burning. The Houthis’ al-Masirah satellite news channel broadcast footage from the aftermath showing bodies at the site.At the time, US central command said, “The strike was not intended to harm the people of Yemen.” The command said the operation was aimed at cutting off fuel supplies and revenue for the Houthis.“US forces took action to eliminate this source of fuel for the Iran-backed Houthi terrorists and deprive them of illegal revenue that has funded Houthi efforts to terrorize the entire region for over 10 years,” US Centcom said in April 2025.The Pentagon review said condolence payments were not considered appropriate for the three strikes, without explaining why. It noted that such payments may be offered following civilian deaths or injuries but are not legally required and do not amount to an admission of wrongdoing.The issue has gained further attention following a US missile strike on an Iranian primary school earlier this year that reportedly killed as many as 168 people. Defence secretary Pete Hegseth has also reportedly reduced the size of a Pentagon office focused on reducing civilian harm.The US began striking the Houthis in 2023 after the group launched attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea, saying it was acting in support of Palestinians during Israel’s war with Hamas.
Article Summary: A Pentagon review says US airstrikes targeting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen killed 153 civilians and injured 243 others across three attacks in April 2025. The assessment, submitted to Congress as part of the Pentagon’s annual civilian casualty report, found that the strikes “more likely than not’ resulted in civilian harm.

Article Title: In 1960, 2-day-old baby David Stevenson was found abandoned in a London flats corridor; 66 years later, he finally discovers his biological family
Article Text:
Abandoned as a baby in 1960, David Stevenson finally discovers his biological family after 66 years.

Becoming a father changed everything for David Stevenson

David says he had no resentment towards his birth mother

DNA helped David find his biological family

David was heartbroken to learn his biological mother had died

‘It was an incredible experience’

David Stevenson has spent more than six decades searching for answers about his past after he was abandoned as a two-day-old baby in London in 1960. He recently appeared on This Morning alongside his cousin Saskia Van Der Hoeven, where he opened up about his extraordinary journey to discover his biological family more than six decades after being abandoned as a baby.Stevenson was found in the corridor on the third floor of a block of flats when he was just two days old. Although his adoptive parents told him from childhood that he had been adopted and found as a baby, he said he did not think much about his past while growing up.Stevenson revealed that his desire to find his biological parents became stronger after he became a father himself. Holding his son for the first time made him think differently about his own story.“As you saw in the programme that was shown last night, it was really the moment when I became a father and I held my son for the first time,” he said.“For a lot of abandoned children and adoptees generally, it’s that moment when it changes from just being you to also being a parent yourself. That really drove me to want to learn more about where I’d come from,” he added.Stevenson also said his adoptive parents were supportive of his decision to search for his biological family.He described his childhood as a happy one and said he had no resentment towards his birth mother.“I always realised that my birth mother must have gone through a very difficult time in her life. She was probably a young woman, and I sort of imagined the circumstances,” he said.Reflecting on the social circumstances of the late 1950s and early 1960s, Stevenson said being an unmarried mother was heavily stigmatised at the time.“In the late 50s, early 60s, you know, being an unwed mother was truly a terrible thing,” he said.He added that the social stigma made it particularly difficult for young women to seek help.“It made it very difficult for young women in that situation to reach out and get help,” Stevenson said.In 2009, Stevenson and his wife also launched a national campaign to find more information about his biological family. Despite investigating people who had lived in the block of flats where he was found and following various clues, the campaign initially failed to produce answers.The breakthrough eventually came through DNA research conducted as part of Long Lost Family. His cousin Saskia Van Der Hoeven explained how the family discovered the connection.According to Van Der Hoeven, the programme’s DNA investigation established a connection to the Netherlands. After her aunt and niece provided DNA samples, the family realised that David’s biological mother was likely Petra, Van Der Hoeven’s aunt.She recalled receiving a phone call from her brother with the unexpected news.“My brother called me and said, ‘Saskia, please sit down. I’ve got something to tell you,’” she recalled.The family then created a group chat called “Rainbow Baby David”. When a photograph and newspaper article about the abandoned baby were shared, Van Der Hoeven said she immediately recognised the connection.“When I saw it, there was no doubt in my mind,” she said.Van Der Hoeven also said Petra had worked as an au pair in France and later in London, which matched the timeline of David’s abandonment.While the DNA discovery finally answered some of his questions, Stevenson faced another emotional revelation: his biological mother had already died.He said meeting his newly discovered relatives in Rotterdam was nevertheless an incredibly meaningful experience. Van Der Hoeven helped him build a picture of the mother he never had the opportunity to meet.“I really got a picture of a woman who was very kind and generous and loving, and it just makes me very sad that I never got to meet her,” Stevenson said.Petra’s sister is still alive and can provide more information about her life and personality, giving Stevenson an opportunity to learn more about his biological mother.Stevenson said his newly discovered family welcomed him warmly, despite having only learned about his existence weeks earlier.“The afternoon we spent together when I met them was such a joy because this family was incredibly welcoming and accepting of me,” he said.“They’d only known about me literally for weeks, whereas I’d had years to come to terms with the idea of a birth mother. So, it was an incredible experience. It really was, and one that will stay with me for the rest of my life,” he added.Stevenson is now planning to return to Rotterdam to meet more of his biological relatives.“I’m planning to go back to Rotterdam in a couple of weeks to meet more of the family, more of my cousins. So, it’s very, very exciting,” he said.For Stevenson, the decades-long search has finally brought a sense of peace and a chance to build new memories with the family he never knew he had.
Article Summary: David Stevenson was abandoned as a two-day-old baby in London in 1960. He has spent more than six decades searching for answers about his past. His cousin Saskia Van Der Hoeven helped him find his biological family. He was heartbroken to learn his biological mother had died.

Article Title: One dead, 172 rescued after Indonesian ferry from Bali catches fire
Article Text:
Smoke from the passenger ferry that caught fire while traveling from the tourist island of Bali to neighboring island of Lombok, AP

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the biggest factor contributing to ferry accidents? Weak safety enforcement Rough weather conditions Poor maintenance of vessels 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

One person died and 172 were rescued after a passenger ferry caught fire in rough seas off Indonesia's Bali island on Wednesday, with rescue operations continuing, authorities said.The Putri Yasmin ferry was carrying passengers and crew when the fire broke out at around 4:15 am while it was travelling from Padang Bai port in Bali to Lembar port on the neighbouring island of Lombok in West Nusa Tenggara province.Authorities said 172 people had been rescued as crews from Indonesian navy ships, patrol boats and rescue vessels battled the blaze. A helicopter was also deployed to conduct an aerial survey of the area.“Our top priority is the safety of all passengers and crew members,” said Muhammad Hariyadi, who heads the Mataram Search and Rescue Office.Hariyadi said rough seas, with waves reaching up to 4 metres (13 feet), were making the rescue operation more difficult.The Mataram Search and Rescue Office received an emergency report nearly 30 minutes after the fire started and immediately sent rescue personnel and vessels to the scene.The ferry was carrying 44 vehicles and 53 motorcycles, according to passenger manifest data released by the Padang Bai port authority.Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries for inter-island travel. Ferry accidents are relatively common in the country, with weak safety enforcement often cited as a contributing factor.
Article Summary: The Putri Yasmin ferry was carrying passengers and crew when the fire broke out at around 4:15 am. It was travelling from Padang Bai port in Bali to Lembar port on the neighbouring island of Lombok. Authorities said 172 people had been rescued as crews from Indonesian navy ships, patrol boats and rescue vessels battled the blaze.

Article Title: Iran knew Trump's hotel floor, targeted his aircraft during Nato summit: Report
Article Text:
The US intercepted intelligence indicating Iran knew Trump's exact location in Ankara and posed a missile threat to his aircraft during the Nato summit, NYT report

The US intercepted several pieces of intelligence indicating Iran knew President Donald Trump’s exact location in Ankara during the Nato summit and that there was a potential threat involving a missile capable of targeting his aircraft, according to a New York Times report.Two US officials familiar with the intelligence told NYT that authorities detected a specific surface-to-air missile threat against whichever aircraft was carrying Trump. Someone near the Nato summit was also reportedly spotted with a shoulder-fired missile, while Iranian operatives were said to know which floor of Trump’s hotel he was staying on.The intelligence was considered serious enough to trigger an elaborate security deception. Trump publicly boarded the older Air Force One, but was then secretly moved out of the airport inside a catering container and transferred to a military aircraft that flew him out of Turkey.The original Air Force One, meanwhile, departed with senior US officials, government employees, journalists and military personnel aboard, apparently serving as a decoy. The passengers were reportedly not informed of the full extent of the threat.The New York Times reported that the operation may have shifted the risk from Trump to those who remained aboard the presidential aircraft. Among them were secretary of state Marco Rubio, treasury secretary Scott Bessent and senior White House aides Stephen Miller and Steven Cheung.The passengers were instructed to keep the plane’s window shades closed during its July 8 flight from Ankara to Britain. Trump later secretly rejoined Air Force One before disembarking in front of cameras, creating the appearance that he had travelled on the aircraft throughout.The unusual manoeuvre has drawn criticism from some former White House officials, who argued that people aboard the decoy aircraft should have been protected or informed. Others defended the decision, saying protecting the president could justify extraordinary measures during a credible threat.The White House did not respond to questions about the operation. Trump later said he had followed Secret Service advice and rejected the suggestion that the passengers had been placed at greater risk, arguing that the aircraft he travelled on may actually have been the more likely target.
Article Summary: US intercepted intelligence indicating Iran knew President Donald Trump’s exact location in Ankara during the Nato summit. There was a potential threat involving a missile capable of targeting his aircraft, according to a New York Times report. The intelligence was considered serious enough to trigger an elaborate security deception. Trump publicly boarded the older Air Force One, but was then secretly moved out of the airport inside a catering container and transferred to a military aircraft.

Article Title: Lake Kariba ferry tragedy: Overcrowding concerns emerge as passenger count remains uncertain
Article Text:
At least 15 people died and 27 remained missing after a passenger ferry capsized on Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba on Tuesday. (@zoleka_zw)

At least 15 people died and 27 remained missing after a passenger ferry capsized on Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba on Tuesday, while 77 people were rescued, authorities said.Questions over possible overcrowding and incomplete passenger records have emerged as authorities work to establish how many people were actually aboard the vessel when it overturned. Ticket records showed 114 adults on board, while five crew members were also listed, putting the recorded total at 119 against the ferry’s stated capacity of 90.Officials, however, said children below the ticketing age may not have been included in the records. This means the actual number of people aboard could have been higher and the current figure of those missing could change as authorities reconcile passenger lists with those rescued and confirmed dead.According to the Associated Press, all 77 rescued passengers reached a small island after the ferry capsized, with boats sent to bring them back. Zimbabwe’s state broadcaster ZBC showed rescue boats operating on the lake, while a helicopter was also deployed. An underwater search team was sent to look for those still unaccounted for.The Civil Protection Unit recommended that the accident be formally declared a disaster.The 114 registered adults and five crew members put the documented number aboard at 119, or 29 above the vessel’s stated capacity. The reported figures of 15 dead, 27 missing and 77 rescued also total 119.However, authorities have not confirmed whether those figures represent the same passenger group reflected in the ticket records. The possibility that children travelled without being included in the records has added further uncertainty.Authorities are now expected to compare passenger records with the names of those rescued, missing and confirmed dead to determine the actual number aboard the ferry.Questions over conditions on the lake had surfaced before the ferry set out. Footage shared by local MP Mutsa Murombedzi showed people on shore expressing concern over whether the vessel could cope with strong waves.Authorities have not linked those warnings to the capsize and have not yet identified weather conditions as the cause of the accident.Murombedzi said the ferry is used by rural communities travelling to Kariba town, with the journey taking about five hours.Lake Kariba lies between Zimbabwe and Zambia and was created following the construction of the Kariba Dam across the Zambezi River in the late 1950s.The accident comes after authorities had previously warned boat operators against carrying more passengers or goods than their vessels were designed to handle.In January 2024, a Water and Inland Department official said overloading had become a concern on Lake Kariba following a series of boat accidents and urged operators to comply with prescribed capacity limits.Safety concerns have continued. Two men died in November 2024 after a small boat carrying three people capsized during a storm. In March 2025, another accident involving a fishing vessel left one person feared dead.Local authorities have repeatedly urged boat users to avoid overloading and exercise caution during poor weather.Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority describes Lake Kariba as the world’s largest man-made lake by volume. At full capacity, it stretches about 282 km, covers around 5,580 sq km and can hold about 185 cubic km of water.The lake is up to 32 km wide at its broadest point, making boats an important transport link for communities along its shores.The immediate focus after Tuesday’s disaster remains the search for the 27 people still missing and determining how many people were actually aboard the ferry when it capsized.
Article Summary: At least 15 people died and 27 are still missing after a passenger ferry capsized on Zimbabwe’s Lake Kariba on Tuesday. Ticket records showed 114 adults on board, while five crew members were also listed, putting the recorded total at 119. Officials, however, said children below the ticketing age may not have been included in the records. This means the actual number of people aboard could have been higher. The Civil Protection Unit recommended that the accident be formally declared a disaster.

Article Title: Decades before Trump’s secret plane swap, Bill Clinton used a decoy to land in Pakistan; reporter reveals how
Article Text:
More than 25 years later, Trump revives Clinton-era flight switch tactic

Trump left, others stayed

Trump acknowledges plane switch

When then-US President Bill Clinton arrived in Islamabad, Pakistan, in March 2000, a decoy aircraft bearing Air Force One markings landed in view of the media, followed by a Secret Service agent resembling Clinton. An unmarked aircraft then landed, carrying the president, who disembarked from it.Susan Page, a White House reporter for USA Today at the time, was among a small group of people who knew about the operation.Before Clinton’s flight from India to Pakistan, White House officials summoned Page, who was then president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, for an off-the-record briefing. White House press and security officials told her about the operation, including Clinton’s location and the safety measures in place for journalists travelling with him, Page told The Washington Post in messages.The briefing meant that at least one journalist travelling with the presidential press corps knew that Clinton would not be aboard Air Force One.“They told me about the extraordinary security procedures being taken because of the dangers in flying there, including use of the decoy plane,” Page was quoted as saying by The Washington Post. “Of course, the dangers threatened the journalists covering the trip as well as President Clinton.”“I haven’t spoken about this episode before, because of the off-the-record ground rules of that discussion,” Page said through a text message. “But since more than a quarter-century has passed — and since the ruse became evident as soon as President Clinton disembarked in Pakistan — I think it’s OK for me to relay it now.”The White House press pool is a rotating group of journalists responsible for reporting on the president’s activities and sharing reports, photographs and video with the wider press corps. The formal system has been in place since 1937, although the White House first used a pool reporter in 1881 after President James Garfield was shot.Associated Press reporter Franklin Trusdell was stationed outside Garfield’s room, monitoring his condition and sharing updates with other journalists.The system is intended to ensure that a member of the press is present to observe the president’s movements and activities, providing the public with an independent account.More than 25 years later, the White House faced a similar security challenge but handled the press differently. Last month, security personnel in Turkey secretly moved President Donald Trump from an aircraft marked as Air Force One to a smaller, unmarked Air Force plane using an airport catering truck. The operation was prompted by a credible Iranian threat to Trump, The Washington Post reported.More than 100 aides, officials and journalists remained aboard the larger Air Force One and continued flying towards Britain, most of them unaware that Trump had secretly switched aircraft on the tarmac, according to a US official.As the aircraft swap took place, reporters aboard the plane were instructed to keep their window shades lowered.Secretary of state Marco Rubio and treasury secretary Scott Bessent, who had accompanied Trump at the Nato summit in Ankara, were among those who stayed aboard the blue-and-white Boeing 747. Other White House staff, military personnel and members of the press also remained on the aircraft, most of them unaware of Trump’s whereabouts.US President Donald Trump has confirmed that he was moved to another aircraft while leaving Turkey last month, saying he followed instructions from the Secret Service and military after being told that the plane he had initially boarded faced a “greater risk”."I go by Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane... I do what they say... I guess there was a threat out there. I didn't really ask too much about it. I get a lot of threats," the US president said."I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk! I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane, I think that they would be more likely to go for it," Trump added.
Article Summary: US President Bill Clinton arrived in Islamabad, Pakistan, in March 2000. A decoy aircraft bearing Air Force One markings landed in view of the media. An unmarked aircraft then landed, carrying the president, who disembarked from it.Susan Page, a White House reporter for USA Today at the time, was among a small group of people who knew about the operation.

Article Title: The United States removed 100 outdated dams in 2025, reconnecting more than 4,893 river miles across 30 states and setting a single-year record for upstream habitat
Article Text:
Dam removal on the Middle Fork Nooksack River, Washington (American Rivers photos)

Why are old dams being removed?

Lower Citico Dam removal, Citico Creek, Tennessee

Restoring wildlife habitat

Cultural importance

The United States removed 100 dams across 30 states in 2025, reconnecting more than 4,893 miles of rivers, according to a report by the organisation American Rivers. The organisation said it was the largest number of upstream river miles reconnected through dam removal in a single year in the US.The removal of these dams has allowed water to flow freely again in places where rivers had been blocked for decades, and in some cases, for centuries. The work is also helping restore access to habitats used by fish and other wildlife.Pennsylvania removed the highest number of dams in the US in 2025, with 14 structures taken out. The state now has 433 documented dam removals since 1912.Other states in the Northeast also recorded significant numbers. Massachusetts removed 11 dams in 2025, while Vermont removed nine. Flooding in both states has highlighted the need to address failing dams and undersized road-stream crossings.Many dams in the US are no longer serving the purpose for which they were originally built. The country has more than 500,000 dams in its national inventory, and many are no longer generating power, supplying water or serving another practical purpose.At the same time, they can affect river ecosystems and public safety.Dams can change the way rivers naturally flow. When a dam blocks a river, it can prevent fish from reaching spawning areas upstream. Water held behind dams can also become warmer and more stagnant. Additionally, some ageing can also create safety risks and increase flooding concerns during storms.Ecology was the most commonly cited reason for dam removal in 2025. It was given as a reason for 59 of the 100 projects completed during the year. Dilapidated or failing structures were the second most common reason, with 37 projects. Safety concerns were cited in 20 projects.The effects can begin soon after a dam is removed. The report said bugs can return within days, while native fish can reach sections of rivers they had been unable to access for generations within weeks.Some of the projects completed in 2025 show how removing a single structure can reconnect large parts of a river system. In Iowa, the Forest City Dam was removed from the Winnebago River. The project reconnected 99 upstream miles for fish passage and opened wetland spawning habitat for northern pike. It also reduced flood risk to a local park.In Delaware, the historic DuPont Experimental Station Dam on the Brandywine River was removed as part of a wider effort involving multiple dams. A previous dam removal upstream in 2019 had already helped change the river. After that project, American shad were seen spawning in the Brandywine in Wilmington for the first time in more than 100 years.The return of the fish showed how river restoration can affect species that had been unable to reach parts of their former habitat for generations.In Virginia, the Georges Mill Dam was removed from the South Mayo River. Seven people had drowned at the site over the years. Removing the dam improved passage for the endangered orangefin madtom and also removed a site that had become a serious safety hazard.Another major project took place in Maine. The removal of Mill Pond Dam on the Sabattus River was part of a wider effort to open access to 2,429 acres of spawning habitat and 75 miles of stream for sea-run fish.The area could support an annual run of more than one million adult alewives. The fish are an important food source for wildlife, including eagles and whales.Dam removal projects are also connected to the cultural practices of Indigenous communities in some places. In California, the Jenny Creek Diversion Dam near the Klamath River was removed by Trout Unlimited and the state Department of Fish and Wildlife. The Yurok Tribe and Shasta Indian Nation also took part in the cleanup and cultural monitoring.A similar restoration effort took place in Utah's Zion National Park, where the Temple of Sinawava Dam was removed. The project was part of an effort to restore the Virgin River, which is a Wild and Scenic River.American Rivers said the 2025 projects also showed the role of local communities, government agencies, conservation groups and Tribal Nations in restoring rivers. It now wants to build on the progress made in 2025 and its target is to remove 30,000 dams by 2050.
Article Summary: Pennsylvania removed the highest number of dams in the US in 2025, with 14 structures taken out. The country has more than 500,000 dams in its national inventory, and many are no longer generating power, supplying water or serving another practical purpose. Ecology was the most commonly cited reason for dam removal in 2025.

Article Title: 'I go by Secret Service, military': Trump confirms switching planes in Turkey over Iran threat
Article Text:
Trump confirms secret flight switch

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think would be most effective in reducing tensions between the US and Iran? Diplomatic talks International mediation 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

US president Donald Trump has acknowledged that he was moved to a different aircraft while leaving Turkey last month, saying he followed instructions from the Secret Service and military after being told the plane he had initially boarded would face a “greater risk”."I go by Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane... I do what they say... I guess there was a threat out there. I didn't really ask too much about it. I get a lot of threats," the US president said."I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk! I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane, I think that they would be more likely to go for it," Trump added.His comments came after a Washington Post report revealed that Trump was secretly transferred from Air Force One to a smaller military aircraft in an airport catering truck amid an alleged Iranian assassination threat.Trump had initially boarded the older, baby-blue Air Force One in full view of cameras after attending the Nato summit in Turkey.Also read: Video shows catering truck used to secretly move Trump between planes amid Iran threat But once aboard, he was secretly transferred in an airport catering truck to an Air Force C-32A, which flew him to Britain, The Washington Post reported, citing a US official familiar with the operation and corroborating material reviewed by the newspaper.Israel had reportedly alerted the United States to the threat that prompted the Secret Service to move Trump off Air Force One and transfer him to a military aircraft as he prepared to leave Turkey, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday, citing an unnamed US official.According to the report, Israeli intelligence indicated that Iran was planning to target Trump’s aircraft with shoulder-fired missiles. Despite the threat, several senior Trump administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, remained aboard Air Force One, the official said.The extraordinary security operation unfolded as hostilities with Iran were escalating. Iran shares a border with Turkey, where Trump had travelled for the NATO summit and made his first international trip aboard a newly renovated aircraft donated by Qatar.The deception operation was triggered by what The Washington Post described as a credible threat to Trump. A similar tactic was used in 2000, when then-President Bill Clinton flew into Pakistan aboard an unmarked executive jet while the official Air Force One aircraft served as a decoy.In this case, journalists who believed they were travelling with Trump aboard the older Air Force One were instructed to keep the window shades in the press cabin closed. Some White House staff members also reportedly believed the president was on board.The C-32A carrying Trump arrived in Britain at around 10:20 pm (local time), with the older Air Force One and the media contingent arriving minutes later, The Post reported. It was not immediately clear how Trump was transferred back to the older Air Force One.
Article Summary: US president Donald Trump says he was moved to a different aircraft while leaving Turkey last month. Trump said he followed instructions from the Secret Service and military after being told the plane he had initially boarded would face a "greater risk" A Washington Post report revealed that Trump was secretly transferred from Air Force One to a smaller military aircraft.

Article Title: From New York to Delaware: US states to commemorate 'India Day' on August 15
Article Text:
US states proclaim August 15 as 'India Day' (representative image)

Delaware honours Indian-American community

New York, New Jersey also recognise August 15

How US communities celebrate India's Independence Day

India marks 80th Independence Day with focus on youth

Delaware has proclaimed August 15, 2026, as ‘India Day’, joining New York and New Jersey in recognising India's Independence Day and the contributions of the Indian-American community ahead of the country's 80th Independence Day.The proclamation was issued by Delaware Governor Matthew Meyer, who highlighted the state's growing Indian-American community and its contributions to the state's social and economic life.The development was shared by the Consulate General of India in New York on August 13.According to the proclamation, Delaware is strengthened by the many cultures and traditions represented across its communities, including its Indian-American population.The proclamation said Delawareans of Indian heritage have enriched the state through their work, leadership and service, contributing to shared prosperity and creating opportunities for future generations.It also highlighted India's diversity of languages, traditions, faiths and customs, noting that generations of Indian Americans have carried these traditions forward while building communities in the US.The proclamation said India Day would provide an opportunity to honour India's independence, celebrate the heritage and achievements of Delaware's Indian-American community and recognise the enduring connections between Delaware and the people of India.Governor Meyer encouraged residents to participate in the observance and recognise the contributions of the state's Indian-American community.Delaware's proclamation follows similar declarations by New York and New Jersey, which recognised August 15, as India's Independence Day.New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill issued a proclamation recognising Indian Independence Day across the state. According to the Consulate General of India in New York, the proclamation highlighted the Indian-American community's contributions to New Jersey in areas including education, healthcare, research, technology, business, public service and community leadership.New York Governor Kathy Hochul also proclaimed August 15 as India Independence Day across the state.The Consulate said New York's proclamation recognised the Indian-American community's contribution to the state's cultural, economic and civic life, while also highlighting the enduring ties between India and the US.The Consulate thanked Hochul for the recognition, saying the proclamation celebrated India's journey of independence and the democratic values shared by the two countries.India's Independence Day is marked across the US each year through flag-hoisting ceremonies, parades, cultural programmes and community events.Indian diplomatic missions, including the Embassy of India in Washington and Indian consulates, hold special programmes on August 15. The Indian mission to the United Nations also participates in commemorative events.Indian-American communities across states organise cultural performances and public celebrations, with local political leaders often participating and highlighting the community's contributions to American society.Prominent landmarks have also joined the celebrations in previous years, including the Empire State Building in New York and the Space Needle in Seattle, which have been illuminated in the colours of the Indian tricolour for Independence Day events.The proclamations come as India prepares to celebrate its 80th Independence Day on August 15, 2026.This year's celebrations will also focus on the commemoration of 150 years of ‘Vande Mataram’, while placing particular emphasis on ‘Yuva Shakti’ or youth power.The celebrations are expected to combine the historical significance of India's freedom movement with recognition of the achievements and contributions of its younger generation.The growing number of US states formally recognising India's Independence Day also underlines the visibility of the Indian-American community and the broader social, economic and cultural ties between India and the United States.
Article Summary: Delaware joins New York and New Jersey in recognising India's Independence Day. Proclamation was issued by Governor Matthew Meyer, who highlighted the state's growing Indian-American community. New York Governor Kathy Hochul also proclaimed August 15 as India Independence Day across the state. The proclamations come as India prepares to celebrate its 80th Independence Day on August 15, 2026.

Article Title: A first in 16 years: US set to execute three death row inmates in single day
Article Text:
The three death row prisoners set for execution on Thursday

Tennessee

Alabama

Oklahoma

The US is set to carry out three executions in a single day on Thursday (local time), marking the first time in 16 years that three people are put to death on the same day in the America.The executions will be carried out in three different states: Tennessee, Alabama, and Oklahoma. The death row prisoners are scheduled to be administered lethal injections.Tennessee plans to execute Anthony Darrell Hines, three months after an attempted lethal injection of another inmate was halted over difficulties inserting an IV line. The failed execution raised concerns over the challenges states can face in establishing IV access.During Tony Carruthers’ attempted execution in May, medical staff established a primary IV line but spent more than an hour trying to insert a required backup line. The execution was eventually called off, and Carruthers received a one-year reprieve.Hines, 66, has argued that his health problems, including two strokes that left him partially paralysed, could make his execution more difficult. He has unsuccessfully sought intervention from the governor and courts, arguing that the doctor who oversaw Carruthers’ attempted execution was "unqualified" and could face similar problems during his execution.Governor Bill Lee has declined to intervene, while the Tennessee Supreme Court last week rejected Hines’ request for a stay. The state has not disclosed whether the same doctor will oversee the process, while the court found Hines had not established that the doctor was unqualified.Hines was convicted of stabbing Catherine Jean Jenkins to death in 1985 while she was working as a motel maid in Kingston Springs. He was sentenced to death in 1986, won an appeal for a new sentencing hearing and received another death sentence in 1989.In Alabama, Jeremy Williams, 42, is scheduled to be for the 2021 rape and murder of 5-year-old Kamarie Holland, a Georgia girl. Williams pleaded guilty and has asked for his death sentence to be carried out.Williams raped and strangled Holland after offering her mother $2,500 for the child to perform a sexual activity. He filmed the assault and kept the victim’s body afterward. He was also charged in 2022 with the 2005 death of his infant daughter in Alaska.If carried out, the execution will be Alabama’s first this year. A nitrogen gas execution was halted in June after a federal judge ruled the method "unconstitutional."Oklahoma is scheduled to execute Carlos Cuesta-Rodriguez, 70, for the 2003 murder of his girlfriend, Olimpia Fisher.Fisher was preparing to leave Cuesta-Rodriguez when he shot her in one eye, waited about eight minutes as she called for help and then fired the fatal shot into her other eye.Oklahoma’s Pardon and Parole Board voted 3-1 last month against recommending clemency. Cuesta-Rodriguez’s lawyers had sought a recommendation for life without parole, citing his troubled childhood and mental health problems, including brain damage, post-traumatic stress disorder and major depression with psychotic episodes.Cuesta-Rodriguez, however, told the board he did not want clemency and wanted Fisher’s two daughters to know that he "regretted" the killing. Speaking through a Spanish-language translator, he expressed "remorse" for what he had done.
Article Summary: Three death row prisoners are scheduled to be administered lethal injections. Tennessee plans to execute Anthony Darrell Hines, three months after an attempted lethal injection of another inmate was halted over difficulties inserting an IV line. Oklahoma is scheduled to execute Carlos Cuesta-Rodriguez, 70, for the 2003 murder of his girlfriend.

Article Title: Missile threat made Donald Trump move to smaller US jet during Turkey visit: Report
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump waves as he switches planes at US Air Force Base in England, on his way back to Washington from the Nato summit in Turkey

Secret Service acted on credible, imminent threat

Air Force One used as a decoy

What kind of missile raised concern?

Journalists on board did not know Trump had left

Questions over 'decoy' plane and passenger safety

Trump had warned of Iran threat

US President Donald Trump was secretly moved to a smaller military aircraft after a credible and imminent threat that a shoulder-fired missile could target his plane during his return from Turkey last month, according to people briefed on the matter cited by Reuters.The extraordinary security operation took place on July 8, the final day of Trump's visit to Ankara for the Nato summit, as tensions with Iran were running high.Trump and a small group of aides were moved from the presidential aircraft to a nondescript C-32A jet using a catering truck, while the larger aircraft continued its journey carrying senior administration officials, White House staff and journalists.The operation was kept secret to conceal the president's movements.According to a person briefed on the matter, the Secret Service determined that the threat was credible and imminent and had little time to prepare an alternative travel plan.A second source told Reuters that there was no clear operational plan by Trump's potential attackers, but there was an apparent intent to target him. That assessment allowed the aircraft to continue flying while additional precautions were taken.The sources did not disclose where the intelligence about the threat came from.Trump confirmed on Tuesday that the Secret Service had ordered him to use a different aircraft, although he did not disclose details of the threat."It's only up to the Secret Service. I just follow what they'd like to do, so I go by Secret Service and the military," Trump told reporters.He added that the aircraft he ultimately travelled on may have been at greater risk because an attacker would have been more likely to target the plane believed to be carrying him."I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk," Trump said. "I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they'd be more likely to go for."Trump had travelled to the Nato summit aboard a newer Boeing 747-8 aircraft gifted by Qatar and retrofitted for US use. For the return journey, however, he had publicly indicated that he would initially use the older Air Force One aircraft.Trump boarded the presidential aircraft in Ankara as expected. He was then secretly moved to a smaller C-32A, a modified Boeing 757 commonly used for senior US officials, through a catering truck.Meanwhile, the larger aircraft departed separately with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House staff and the travelling press corps.The operation was designed to make it appear that Trump was still aboard the presidential aircraft.Rubio was aware of the aircraft switch and the threat behind it. A senior US official told news agency AP that Bessent was likely aware of the situation, although the official could not confirm it.Trump's security arrangements were more extensive because of the specific threat to the president, the official said.The nature of the reported threat has not been publicly confirmed by US officials.Douglas Birkey, executive director of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Reuters that one possibility was a newer type of heat-seeking missile designed to home in on an aircraft's hot engines.Such weapons can be difficult to detect because they do not necessarily emit the radio signals associated with radar-guided systems.Birkey cited the Iranian SA-67 as one possible example, describing it as a weapon believed to have heat-seeking and laser-guidance capabilities. He also pointed to Russia's shoulder-launched 9K333 Verba system.However, there has been no public confirmation that either weapon was involved in the threat against Trump.The secrecy of the operation meant that journalists and some White House staff travelling on the larger aircraft were unaware that Trump had been moved to another plane.The Washington Post first reported details of the operation this week, more than a month after it took place. The New York Times subsequently reported that US intelligence officials had been concerned that Iranian operatives knew where Trump was staying in Ankara, including the floor of his hotel.Journalists aboard the aircraft were instructed to keep the window shades closed. The White House Correspondents' Association later said members of the travelling press noticed unusual security arrangements around the plane.Trump eventually flew to a refuelling stop in Britain without incident and later transferred back to the legacy presidential aircraft before continuing his journey to the US.The operation has raised questions about the safety of those who remained aboard the aircraft believed to be carrying the president.Among those passengers were senior members of Trump's Cabinet as well as journalists.Some commentators and lawmakers have questioned whether using the presidential aircraft as a decoy could have exposed those passengers to danger if an attack had occurred.The Reuters source said officials nevertheless determined that concealing Trump's movements was in his best interests given the heightened tensions with Iran.Presidential security is treated differently from that of even the most senior Cabinet officials.Under the US Constitution, the secretary of state and secretary of the treasury are among those in the presidential line of succession, but they do not receive the same level of protection as the president.The incident came against the backdrop of heightened US-Iran tensions and renewed American military action against Iran.Trump had previously said that he was a major target for Iran and acknowledged on Tuesday that he regularly receives threats."I guess there was a threat out there," Trump said, according to the BBC's earlier report. "I didn't really ask too much about it. I get a lot of threats."He added, "I have a lot of threats that you don't know about."US presidents have previously travelled secretly during high-risk trips, particularly during visits to war zones.But the Turkey operation was unusual because it involved creating the appearance that Trump remained aboard one aircraft while secretly moving him to another, with members of the travelling press corps unaware of the switch.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump was secretly moved to a smaller military aircraft after a credible and imminent threat that a shoulder-fired missile could target his plane. The extraordinary security operation took place on July 8, the final day of Trump's visit to Ankara for the Nato summit, as tensions with Iran were running high.

Article Title: US law enforcement to target 'transnational criminal organistaions' with cyber tools
Article Text:
Trump expands cyber tools for US law enforcement

US president Donald Trump signed a memorandum on Wednesday aimed at expanding federal law enforcement’s use of cyber tools against transnational criminal organisations operating abroad, the White House said.Trump signed a national security presidential memorandum directing his administration to “leverage the capability and innovation of the private sector to help conduct these cyber operations under the direction, control, and authority of the US Government,” the White House said, as cited by Reuters.The White House, in a fact sheet on the memorandum, cited ransomware attacks, financial fraud and other crimes carried out by foreign-based criminal organisations, which the memo refers to as “transnational criminal organizations.”The memo directs the department of homeland security, through the Homeland Security Task Force’s National Coordination Center, to establish a programme “to conduct specific cyber operations that disrupt foreign TCOs”, under the oversight of DHS and the Department of Justice.The memo sets out a framework for private-sector companies to work with other private entities and federal, state, local, tribal and territorial agencies to collect intelligence on transnational criminal organisations and recommend cyber operations to tackle the threats they pose, the White House said.According to the memo, vetted participating companies will, under federal government supervision, carry out “cyber surveillance operations” and “cyber effects operations” against designated targets."Cyber effects includes ‌the potential manipulation, disruption, denial, degradation, or destruction of information systems, networks, physical or virtual infrastructure controlled by information systems, or ​information resident thereon," ​the memo stated.According to the memo, participating companies will be required to maintain a bond or escrow of at least $1 million. The involvement of private-sector firms in cyber operations against criminal and other targets is not new and has previously drawn controversy over concerns about escalation, unintended consequences and coordination between agencies.
Article Summary: US president Donald Trump signed a memorandum on Wednesday aimed at expanding federal law enforcement’s use of cyber tools against transnational criminal organisations operating abroad. The memo directs the department of homeland security to establish a programme “to conduct specific cyber operations that disrupt foreign TCOs”

Article Title: Indian-origin teen charged with murdering mother, brother in US after ‘kill family’ searches
Article Text:
Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts.

A 17-year-old Indian-origin teenager has been charged with allegedly murdering his mother and younger brother at their home in Acton, Massachusetts, authorities said.The teen has been charged with two counts of murder, two counts each of assault and battery on a household or family member and assault and battery, along with charges of using a vehicle without authority and stealing a motor vehicle.The 17-year old is accused of fatally assaulting his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his 14-year-old brother, Siddharth Aravind, inside their Martha Lane home on Tuesday before fleeing in his mother's car.Middlesex district attorney Marian Ryan and acton police chief Douglas Sturniolo said police received a call from teen's father shortly after 6.37 pm on August 11 after he was unable to contact his family. A tutor expected at the house had also been unable to reach anyone.The father had last spoken to Sudha early Tuesday morning before leaving for work, while Siddharth was last seen around noon, authorities said.Police who arrived at the house found both victims dead. Siddharth was found on the first floor and Sudha in the finished basement. Both victims were found with “obvious trauma”, but the chief medical examiner has yet to release information on the exact cause and manner of death.The type of weapon used in the killings is also still under investigation.The accused was not at the house when police arrived and was believed to have fled in his mother's vehicle. Investigators issued an alert for him as they searched for the teenager.He was found early Wednesday in the vehicle in a parking lot in Wayland, Massachusetts, after local police responded to an unrelated alarm. He was taken into custody without incident.The Middlesex county district attorney's office said investigators found that Arjun had recently displayed concerning behaviour."The subsequent investigation indicates that Arjun had recently been demonstrating concerning behaviour, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasies regarding killing his family,” the statement said.Arjun was expected to be arraigned in Lowell juvenile court on Wednesday. However, the juvenile court does not have jurisdiction over murder charges. He will therefore face arraignment on the murder and related assault charges in Concord district court later.
Article Summary: Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts. The 17-year-old is accused of fatally assaulting his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his brother, Siddharth Aravind, 14. The teen has been charged with two counts of murder, two counts each of assault and battery.

Article Title: 30 senators flag delays in US visa appointments for Indian students
Article Text:
The senators said delays could prevent students and exchange visitors from reaching the US in time for the beginning of the academic year

With the US fall academic season weeks away, a shortage of timely student-visa appointments has emerged as a growing concern for international students, including Indians, with 30 US senators now pressing the state department to explain delays in processing F, M and J visas. These are visas for academic studies, vocational courses and exchange programmes, respectively.In a letter dated Aug 11, senator Alex Padilla and 29 other senators told US secretary of state Marco Rubio that they were hearing from students and other stakeholders that “no timely visa appointments are available” at several US embassies and consulates.The senators said delays could prevent students and exchange visitors from reaching the US in time for the beginning of the academic year. They have asked the state department to explain how interview appointments are being allocated, where student and exchange visas rank among the department’s priorities, and whether F, M and J applicants have been deprioritised.“We urge the state department to extend interview waivers for vetted returning student applicants; ensure adequate staffing for timely visa vetting and processing; and meaningfully engage with stakeholders to promote greater transparency,” states the letter.The letter also seeks data on staffing levels, average visa-processing times at the five posts processing the largest number of student and exchange-visitor visas, and the number of applications refused following enhanced vetting.The intervention comes at a sensitive time for Indian students heading to US universities for the fall 2026 intake. While Open Doors data does not provide a country-wise analysis of new student enrolments, the Indian contingent has been traditionally significant in numbers. During the academic year 2024-25, the US housed 3.6 lakh students from India.Immigration attorneys state that staffing crunches and rigorous interviews, which entail checking of social media accounts, have led to unprecedented delays. Online discussions among Indian F-1 applicants indicate that securing an appointment has now become a significant concern.
Article Summary: 30 US senators are pressing the state department to explain delays in processing F, M and J visas. These are visas for academic studies, vocational courses and exchange programmes.
